Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

vignette:
Declan Marsh is a 29-year-old Coast Guard petty officer of Irish and Polish descent who lives with his long-term partner on the outskirts of a coastal town in New England. He presented for psychological assessment following a referral from his unit's medical officer, though the events that brought him to this point began nearly fourteen months ago, on a night he still cannot fully account for in words.

It was a Thursday evening in late autumn. Declan had finished a long shift and stopped at a convenience store near the waterfront on his way home. The parking lot was poorly lit, and as he returned to his truck he was approached by two men. What followed lasted perhaps four minutes, though he has no reliable sense of that duration. One of the men produced a knife. Declan was struck from behind, shoved against the hood of his vehicle, and held there while his wallet, phone, and keys were taken. The cold metal of the hood pressed against his cheek. At some point he registered the sound of footsteps retreating. Then he was alone in the parking lot, standing without knowing how he had come to be standing.

In the weeks after the incident, Declan found himself unable to do what seemed like the simplest thing: tell his partner what had happened. Not because he was unwilling, but because when he tried, the words simply did not organise themselves into anything coherent. He could open his mouth and produce nothing that felt like an account. He knew something had happened to him, but the shape of it resisted language. His partner, Nora, would ask gentle questions, and Declan would sit across from her at the kitchen table looking, she later told him, as though he were watching a film in a language he didn't speak. On some occasions he could recount a sequence of events in a flat, detached tone that seemed to disturb Nora more than silence - a recitation that felt to him as though he were describing something that had happened to a person he had read about, someone with his name but no claim on him. At other times what came to him were not scenes at all but pieces: the specific grain of the truck's hood beneath his palm, a smell he could not identify, the weight of stillness after the footsteps stopped. These fragments arrived without context and without connection to each other, and he had come to believe that his inability to assemble them into a coherent whole meant something was fundamentally wrong with his mind.

Declan's work as a Coast Guard petty officer placed him regularly in environments that intersected with these unresolved fragments in ways he found difficult to manage. Patrol shifts along the waterfront - the same general geography as the parking lot - required him to function with authority and composure in poorly lit outdoor spaces at night, and he was certain that his colleagues had noticed something altered in him, though no one had said so directly. He began volunteering for daytime administrative duties in a way that struck his supervisor as out of character for someone who had previously preferred active deployment. Over the months, this quiet repositioning had begun to affect his standing and his own sense of professional identity.

At home, the distance between Declan and Nora had widened in ways neither of them had fully named. He was present but unreachable on certain evenings - not hostile, simply absent in a way that Nora described as like talking to someone through glass. She had eventually suggested, with care, that he speak to someone. He had agreed, though what frightened him most was not the prospect of revisiting the event but the possibility that the fragmentation itself was permanent - that the pieces would never cohere, that he would spend the rest of his life in possession of an experience he could not actually hold.

What finally brought him to the intake appointment was a moment during a routine night patrol when he stood at the edge of a dock, looked out at the dark water, and realised he could not remember the drive there. He made the call to the medical officer the following morning.
